title: Young trumpeter Don Reinberg and sitting in at Snookie's
summary: Brushing up his reading with 20-year-old Don Reinberg, a legit player amazed that Jones could play "Stardust" without music; after the show Jones sat in with Earl Hines at Snookie's on 46th Street.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Everything -- everybody's in here. So now I go to rehearsal and I play, and I found out, well, I've got to brush up a little. I've got a little 20 year old Jewish boy, Don Reinberg, I'll never forget him. This guy could play the thing down like he'd been playing it for years. He just got out of the Army, and his father was a cellist in Seattle -- no, in San Francisco. And he could play this legit music, oh, God. He'd run down it, and he'd get a little frightened on the high notes, but otherwise, he was straight. But what happened is -- he was a wonderful kid. I used to take him around with me at night, because I got so that playing that thing every night, it's beautiful, and you hear beautiful music every night, but you start to wonder if I can play jazz anymore, you know?

And then I would go out. Sometimes I would go and sit in with Earl, over on 46th, at Snookie's. You know, just when I'd get off, when the show let out. The let out at 11:15, and I'd take him with me. And he couldn't understand that. Don Reinberg would say, 'I can't understand how you can walk into another band like that, close your eyes and start playing 'Stardust,' with no music or nothing.' And he said, 'Them notes that you play all night, how do you think them things up?' See, he never played any jazz or anything. Everything was just legit, you know, and stuff. And he enjoyed that. And right now, if he sees I'm playing somewhere and that
band is travelling, coming through town, he'll stop by to see me and say hello, or else he'll leave a note in my box.
46th Street close to 6th Avenue. I don't know what it's called now, but it was closer to 6th Avenue than it was 7th.
